## P.3 Historically: How the McGucken Duality Came to Be Recognized

Historically, the McGucken Duality is the pattern that foundational physics has been articulating in fragments for two centuries, without recognizing what it was, until the McGucken framework supplied the source principle dx₄/dt = ic from which the dual-channel architecture descends.

The historical pattern is uniform and traceable across sixteen catalogued sightings (Hamilton-Lagrange, Schrödinger 1926b's documented suppression of Hamilton's the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel, Heisenberg-Schrödinger 1925-26, Heisenberg-picture-Schrödinger-picture, Feynman-Dyson, Wightman-Haag-Kastler, canonical-geometric quantisation, Wheeler-Feynman retarded-advanced, Bohr complementarity, Ashtekar connection-metric, Hertz 1894 stripping of Maxwell, Einstein's QM/GR channel split, Riemann-Hilbert spectral-dynamical, Harlow 2026 path-integral-knows-more, Turok 2024 cosmological-constant-and-arrow-of-time, Tong 2024 gauge-redundancy-and-discreteness-continuity), with the pattern documented in §IV.A of the present paper. The historical layers are:

### P.3.1 Hamilton-Lagrange (1834-1843): the first dual derivational chains

Hamilton's canonical equations $\dot q = \partial H/\partial p$, $\dot p = -\partial H/\partial q$ and Lagrange's principle of stationary action $\delta S = 0$ supplied two disjoint derivational chains for the same classical equations of motion. The Legendre transform $H = p\dot q - L$ connected them. The Hamilton-Jacobi equation was the third reading on the same structure. This was the first historical articulation of dual derivational chains for the same physics. What Hamilton and Lagrange did not have: the source principle from which both chains descend.

### P.3.2 Schrödinger 1926b's documented suppression of Hamilton's geometric the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel

When Schrödinger derived the wave equation from Hamilton's geometric-variational reading, he explicitly noted in 1926b that the orthodox tradition had suppressed Hamilton's geometry in favor of the algebraic-canonical content. This is documented in Schrödinger's own primary-source writings — he saw the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel-suppressing-dx₄/dt=ic the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel pattern in real time, named it, and proceeded with both readings. The orthodox tradition continued to suppress Hamilton's the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel for the subsequent 95 years.

### P.3.3 Heisenberg-Schrödinger 1925-1926: matrix mechanics vs wave mechanics

Matrix mechanics (Heisenberg 1925) and wave mechanics (Schrödinger 1926) supplied two distinct formulations of quantum mechanics. Schrödinger 1926 proved their formal equivalence. Dirac 1927 unified them through transformation theory. The Heisenberg-picture and Schrödinger-picture versions of QM are dual to this day. Neither Heisenberg nor Schrödinger identified the equivalence as evidence of a principle; the orthodox community came to favor Heisenberg-Dirac algebraic formalism for QFT, keeping the Schrödinger-wave-mechanical-geometric account as a teaching tool rather than as source.

**Remark P.3.3.1 (Historical Case: Heisenberg-Schrödinger 1925-1926 as the founding QM instance of the geometry/algebra channel split).** *The Heisenberg-Schrödinger 1925-1926 case is the historical founding instance of the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic-Channel and dx₄/dt=ic Geometric-Channel split of the McGucken framework at the QM level. Three points of the historical record deserve documentation with primary and scholarly sourcing.*

*(i) The two derivations proceeded from partially overlapping but primarily different empirical starting data.* Heisenberg's July 1925 paper [Heisenberg 1925, "Über quantentheoretische Umdeutung kinematischer und mechanischer Beziehungen," Zeitschrift für Physik 33, 879-893] targeted spectrograph output — the frequencies and intensities of atomic emission spectral lines as read from photographic plates. The primary observational commitment was the Ritz combination principle of Walther Ritz 1908 [Ritz, W. 1908, "On a new law of series spectra," Astrophysical Journal 28, 237-243], which formulated the observed regularity that certain pairs of spectral-line frequencies add: $\nu(i,j) + \nu(j,k) = \nu(i,k)$. Connes 2000 [Connes, A. 2000, "Noncommutative Geometry Year 2000," arXiv math/0011193, §III on Quantum Mechanics] states the observational content of Heisenberg's derivation verbatim: "quantum mechanics showed that indeed the parameter space, or phase space of the mechanical system given by a single atom fails to be a manifold. It is important to convince oneself of this fact and to understand that this conclusion is indeed dictated by the *experimental findings of spectroscopy*." Connes' account of Heisenberg's own path to the matrix content is verbatim: "What Heisenberg understood, by analogy with the classical treatment of the interaction of a mechanical system with the electromagnetic field, is that this Ritz-Rydberg combination principle actually dictates an algebraic formula for the product of any two observable physical quantities attached to the atomic system... Heisenberg didn't know about matrices, he just worked it out, but he was told later by Born, Jordan and Dirac that the algebra he had worked out was known to mathematicians as the algebra of matrices." Europhysics News 2025 [Europhysics News 56/2, "1925: the first papers on quantum mechanics"] gives the empirical target explicitly: "Heisenberg aimed to construct a theory for calculating spectroscopic quantities, that is the frequencies and intensities of the spectral lines of atomic and molecular systems... He called these spectroscopic quantities observable and contrasted them with the unobservable quantities describing the motion of the electrons within these microscopic systems."

Schrödinger's four 1926 papers [Schrödinger 1926a-d, "Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem," Annalen der Physik 79, 361; 79, 489; 80, 437; 81, 109] targeted a theoretical construct rather than a new empirical measurement: de Broglie's matter-wave hypothesis of 1924 [de Broglie, L. 1924, "Recherches sur la théorie des Quanta," Doctoral thesis, University of Paris]. Verbatim from arXiv 2202.07838 (Quantization: History and Problems): "In his 1924 Ph.D. thesis, Louis de Broglie had postulated the existence of a matter wave associated with every matter particle, inspired by Albert Einstein's earlier (1905) proposal that there may be photons, or particles of light, associated with classical electromagnetic waves. Erwin Schrödinger sought to determine how de Broglie's matter waves could be defined in general, and what their dynamics might be." The Zurich-seminar prompt of late 1925 — Peter Debye's remark that "if there is a wave, there should be a wave equation to describe it" — is recorded in the historical literature as the immediate proximate cause of Schrödinger's derivation. The empirical benchmark to reproduce was Bohr's hydrogen energy spectrum; the starting-point of the derivation was theoretical (a hypothesis about wave-particle symmetry) and mathematical (the Hamilton-Jacobi analogy of classical mechanics). Schrödinger built the wave equation by Hamilton-Jacobi analogy and checked at the end that the eigenvalues match the hydrogen spectrum. Verbatim from arXiv 0806.4515 (The Rise of Quantum Mechanics): "Schrödinger took advantage of the analogy between the wave propagation and the motion of a particle already explored by de Broglie in his thesis and even earlier by William Rowan Hamilton (1805-1865) in 1824."

The two derivations converged on the same theorem (the Bohr hydrogen spectrum, correctly reproducing the empirically-measured Balmer, Lyman, Paschen series) from different empirical foundations: line-intensity measurements on photographic plates on the Heisenberg side; the de Broglie matter-wave hypothesis together with the Hamilton-Jacobi analogy on the Schrödinger side. Muller 1997 [Muller, F.A. 1997, "The equivalence myth of quantum mechanics — Parts I and II," Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics 28, 35-61 and 219-247] and Madrid-Casado 2008 [ScienceDirect S1355219808000063, "Why were Matrix Mechanics and Wave Mechanics considered equivalent?"] both record the empirical divergence verbatim: "In addition, the formalisms were initially applied to two distinct sets of experimental results."

*(ii) The two physicists came from substantially different mathematical backgrounds.* Heisenberg was trained under Arnold Sommerfeld at Munich and Max Born at Göttingen in the Bohr-Sommerfeld semi-classical perturbation-theory tradition, using action-angle variables and Fourier expansion of classical orbits. The Kramers-Heisenberg dispersion formula of 1925 — Heisenberg's own precursor work — was formulated in this classical action-angle framework. Heisenberg himself did not know matrix theory when he wrote his July 1925 paper, per the Connes verbatim quote above. Born, whose earlier training under Jakob Rosanes had included matrix algebra, and who was familiar with Hilbert's spectral theory of integral equations, recognized the matrix structure of Heisenberg's multiplication rule after seeing the manuscript. Madrid-Casado (UNESCO/EOLSS, Mathematical History of Wave and Matrix Quantum Mechanics) records the historical moment verbatim: "Those square arrays Q and P were matrices, as Born and Jordan (1925) indicated. Heisenberg did not really arrange his quantum-theoretical quantities into a table or array. He began to deal with sets of allowed physical quantities. But Born looked at these sets of numbers and he suddenly saw that they could be interpreted as mathematical matrices. Furthermore, Born could not take his mind off Heisenberg's symbolic rule for multiplying kinematic quantities, and after a time of intensive thought and trial he suddenly remembered an algebraic theory which he had learned from his [former teacher, Jakob Rosanes]." The full mathematical formalization was completed in Born-Jordan 1925 ["Zur Quantenmechanik," Zeitschrift für Physik 34, 858-888] and Born-Heisenberg-Jordan 1926 ["Zur Quantenmechanik II," Zeitschrift für Physik 35, 557-615, the "Drei-Männer-Arbeit"].

Schrödinger was trained in Vienna in the Boltzmann statistical-mechanics tradition, extensively grounded in classical continuum mechanics, wave optics, Hamilton-Jacobi mechanics, and Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue theory of PDEs. He collaborated with the mathematician Hermann Weyl at ETH Zurich on the mathematics of his wave-mechanics papers. Verbatim from historical secondary source (galileo-unbound.blog, "100 Years of Quantum Physics: Schrödinger's Wave Mechanics"): Schrödinger "went back to first principles, to the classical theory of Hamiltonian mechanics, identifying Hamilton's characteristic function with the phase of an electron wave and deriving a non-relativistic equation using variational principles subject to boundary conditions. The eigenvalues of this new equation, when applied to hydrogen, matched the Bohr spectrum perfectly!"

The mathematical inheritances are two distinct traditions. Heisenberg descended from Bohr-Sommerfeld action-angle perturbation theory and (via Born's post-hoc recognition) from the Cayley matrix-algebra tradition of 1858 and Hilbert's integral-equation spectral theory of 1904-1910. Schrödinger descended from the Hamilton-Jacobi mechanics of 1824-1834, the Sturm-Liouville PDE eigenvalue theory of 1836-1837, and classical wave optics of Huygens 1678 and Fresnel 1818. Hilbert himself remarked on the algebra-vs-wave-picture distinction to Born and Heisenberg months before Schrödinger's paper. Verbatim from arXiv 2511.07502 (per Edward Condon's recollection): "Hilbert, whose intuition about mathematics often preceded its formalization, remarked that matrices had appeared naturally in his own work when solving boundary-value problems in differential equations. In those cases, the matrix elements represented relationships between wave-like functions, and their eigenvalues corresponded to measurable quantities, such as frequencies or energies. He suggested, with characteristic simplicity, that they might try to find the differential equation whose eigenvalues generated those matrices — in essence, to look for the wave picture behind the algebraic symbols. To Born and Heisenberg, however, this sounded like a retreat into classical imagery. Their matrix mechanics was meant to abandon continuous pictures entirely; to invoke a differential equation seemed to miss the point. They politely dismissed Hilbert's idea. Only a few months later, Erwin Schrödinger derived a wave equation that described the same quantized energy levels as Heisenberg's matrices." Condon's account records Hilbert as having laughed at Born and Heisenberg on hearing of Schrödinger's result, remarking that they could have anticipated Schrödinger's derivation six months earlier if only they had followed his advice.

*(iii) Schrödinger and Heisenberg both named the division themselves, in print and in correspondence.* In the opening of Schrödinger 1926e (the equivalence paper), Schrödinger characterized Heisenberg's method with the phrase "transcendental algebra." The fuller verbatim quote reads: "I was discouraged, if not repulsed, by what seemed to me very difficult methods of transcendental algebra, defying any visualisation" (Schrödinger 1926e, Ann. Phys. 384(8), 734-756; also documented in the IMUS Sevilla archive of Schrödinger's remarks). The complaint has two components — the objection is to a *method* (algebraic), and its ground is absence of *Anschaulichkeit* (visualizability). Verbatim from the arXiv 0909.3258 rendering: "I naturally knew about his [Heisenberg's] theory, but was discouraged by what appeared to me as very difficult methods of transcendental algebra."

Heisenberg's mirror position is documented in his letter to Pauli of 8 June 1926, verbatim: "The more I think about the physical part of Schrödinger's theory, the more disgusting I find it," and "What Schrödinger writes about the Anschaulichkeit of his theory, ... I consider Mist" [Heisenberg to Pauli, 8 June 1926, in Pauli, W. (ed. Hermann, A., v. Meyenn, K., Weisskopf, V.F.) 1979, *Wissenschaftlicher Briefwechsel*, Springer, p. 328]. The German word "Mist" is variously translated by commentators: "junk" (Miller 1982), "rubbish" (Beller 1999), "crap" (Cassidy 1992), and, per de Regt 1997, more literally "bullshit." Heisenberg's disgust was with Schrödinger's Anschaulichkeit-claim specifically, which is the geometric-visualizable side of the dichotomy against Heisenberg's algebraic-operational side.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy [SEP, "The Uncertainty Principle," Section 1] summarizes the contrast verbatim: "Even so, the two approaches differed greatly in interpretation and spirit. Whereas Heisenberg eschewed the use of visualizable pictures, and accepted discontinuous transitions as a primitive notion, Schrödinger claimed as an advantage of his theory that it was anschaulich. In Schrödinger's vocabulary, this meant that the theory represented the observational data by means of continuously evolving causal processes in space and time. He considered this condition of Anschaulichkeit to be an essential requirement on any acceptable physical theory."

Heisenberg later reclaimed the term in his 1927 uncertainty paper [Heisenberg, W. 1927, "Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik" ("On the anschaulich content of quantum theoretical kinematics and mechanics"), Zeitschrift für Physik 43, 172-198]. Verbatim from SEP on this reclamation: "He started by redefining the notion of Anschaulichkeit. Whereas Schrödinger associated this term with the provision of a causal space-time picture of the phenomena, Heisenberg, by contrast, declared: 'We believe we have gained anschaulich understanding of a physical theory, if in all simple cases, we can grasp the experimental consequences qualitatively and see that the theory does not lead to any contradictions.'" Heisenberg's 1927 move was to redefine visualizability itself into an operational sense (qualitative-grasp-of-experimental-consequences) that his algebraic apparatus could satisfy, rather than Schrödinger's spatio-temporal sense that only geometric-wave content can supply. The founders named the division themselves — Heisenberg is the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel, Schrödinger the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel — on their own written testimony in 1926 correspondence, in the 1926 equivalence paper's opening, and in Heisenberg's 1927 uncertainty paper title reclaiming and redefining the term.

Muller 1997 and Madrid-Casado 2008 both frame the historical situation with the algebra-vs-differential-equation contrast verbatim: "The Matrix Mechanics was an algebraic approach employing the technique of manipulating matrices. The Wave Mechanics, in contrast, employed differential equations and had a basic partial differential wave equation at its heart. In addition, the formalisms were initially applied to two distinct sets of experimental results." Schrödinger's own equivalence paper of 1926e ["Über das Verhältnis der Heisenberg-Born-Jordanschen Quantenmechanik zu der meinen," Annalen der Physik 79, 734-756] opens with the verbatim statement: "Considering the extraordinary differences between the starting-points and the concepts of Heisenberg's quantum mechanics and of the theory which has been designated 'undulatory' or 'physical' mechanics, and has lately been described here, it is very strange that these new two theories agree with one another with regard to the known facts, where they differ from the old quantum theory... starting-points, presentations, methods and in fact the whole mathematical apparatus, seem fundamentally different."

*The Heisenberg-Schrödinger 1925-1926 case is therefore the historical founding instance of the pattern the McGucken framework catalogs at 47 theorems in §IX.30.C.1 below: two derivations converging on the same physical statement (the Bohr hydrogen spectrum) from disjoint mathematical apparatuses (matrix algebra with Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization on the Heisenberg side; Hamilton-Jacobi mechanics with Sturm-Liouville PDE eigenvalue theory on the Schrödinger side) starting from different empirical starting-data (line-intensity spectrograph measurements on the Heisenberg side; the de Broglie matter-wave hypothesis on the Schrödinger side). Schrödinger 1926e's proof of formal equivalence between the two formulations — via identification of matrix elements with integrals of wave functions over configuration space — is the first historical instance of a convergent-overdetermination proof for a QM theorem. The dual-derivation pattern was present at the birth of QM.*

*What the McGucken framework adds beyond the 1926 recognition. (a) Identification of dx₄/dt = ic as the single source principle from which both channels descend, with the algebraic side generated through Stone's theorem on the one-parameter unitary group $U(t) = e^{-i\hat H t/\hbar}$ and the geometric side generated through iterated McGucken-Sphere expansion with Compton-phase accumulation. (b) Extension of the two-channel structure beyond QM to GR (Hilbert 1915 variational route + Jacobson 1995 thermodynamic route to the Einstein field equations; §IX.10 above), to thermodynamics (Two-Tier Architecture; [MG-Time-Arrows, 2026, Theorem 5.1]), and to cosmology. (c) The 47-theorem catalog of §IX.30.C.1 as documentation of the pattern across QM and GR sectors. (d) The content-asymmetry theorem of §IX.30.C.2 (the seventeen mono-channel items the algebraic apparatus cannot reach, including the strict Second Law of thermodynamics, the arrow of time, and the +ic orientation itself). (e) Identification of this dual-channel architecture as the specific case of the mathematics-wide geometry/algebra distinction traced from Euclid 300 BCE through Descartes 1637 to the twentieth-century axiomatic tradition (§P.1.4.D above). The Heisenberg-Schrödinger 1925-1926 case is prior art for the convergent-overdetermination pattern instantiated at one QM theorem (hydrogen spectrum); the McGucken framework identifies the pattern as ubiquitous across foundational physics and identifies dx₄/dt = ic as the source principle.*

*Scholarly caveat on the equivalence claim. Muller 1997 argued that the 1920s consensus on Heisenberg-Schrödinger equivalence rested on an ontologically-specific proof (matching hydrogen energy levels, not general Hilbert-space isomorphism), with the rigorous general isomorphism established only in von Neumann 1932 [von Neumann, J. 1932, Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik, Springer]. The Stone-von Neumann uniqueness theorem [Stone 1930, von Neumann 1931] later provided the finite-degree-of-freedom uniqueness result. In infinite degrees of freedom (QFT), three independent lines of work establish that the two pictures diverge in ways the finite-dimensional equivalence proofs do not cover. First, Haag's theorem [Haag 1955] establishes that inequivalent representations of the canonical commutation relations exist in QFT. Second, the categorical inequivalence result of Johnson-Freyd 2021 [Johnson-Freyd, T. 2021, "Heisenberg-Picture Quantum Field Theory," in *Representation Theory, Mathematical Physics, and Integrable Systems: In Honor of Nicolai Reshetikhin*, Progress in Mathematics Vol. 340, pp. 371-409, Birkhäuser/Springer; arXiv:1508.05908] establishes at the categorical level that the Schrödinger picture is captured by Atiyah-Segal-type functors while the Heisenberg picture requires factorization-algebra or skein-theory structure with target categories of pointed vector spaces or associative algebras. Third, Dirac himself in 1965 [Dirac, P.A.M. 1965, "Quantum Electrodynamics without Dead Wood," Physical Review 139(3B), pp. B684-B690] — the physicist who had unified matrix mechanics and wave mechanics via transformation theory in 1927 — raised the inequivalence of the two pictures in QED. Verbatim from the Dirac 1965 abstract: "The inference is that the Heisenberg picture is a good picture, the Schrödinger picture is a bad picture, and the two pictures are not equivalent. The usual proof of the equivalence of the two pictures fails because the state vector of the Schrödinger picture does not remain in Hilbert space." Bédard 2025 [Bédard, C.A. 2025, arXiv:2510.02138, forthcoming in Ney (ed.), *Local Quantum Mechanics*, Oxford University Press] extends the inequivalence to the realism level: descriptors surject onto but do not reduce to the Schrödinger state, and the two structures are non-isomorphic. The McGucken framework's dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic-Channel and dx₄/dt=ic Geometric-Channel distinction extends and refines the Heisenberg-Schrödinger split by identifying dx₄/dt = ic as the source principle and by extending the split beyond QM to GR, thermodynamics, and cosmology, with the derivational disjointness criterion of Definition IX.26.2 above supplying the mathematical criterion that the historical Heisenberg-Schrödinger case instantiates.*

**Remark P.3.3.2 (Dirac's unpublished geometric route: primary-source evidence that the QM unifier worked geometrically and published algebraically).** *Paul A.M. Dirac — the physicist who unified matrix mechanics and wave mechanics through transformation theory [Dirac, P.A.M. 1927, "The Physical Interpretation of the Quantum Dynamics," Proceedings of the Royal Society A 113, 621-641], the physicist who derived the relativistic wave equation for the electron [Dirac 1928, "The Quantum Theory of the Electron," Proc. Roy. Soc. A 117, 610-624], and the physicist whose 1930 textbook* Principles of Quantum Mechanics *placed the abstract Hilbert-space formulation of QM in the form it retains today — trained in projective geometry under Peter Fraser at the University of Bristol from 1918-1921, and by his own testimony worked geometrically while publishing algebraically.*

*Direct primary-source evidence from Dirac's 30 October 1972 Boston University lecture "Projective Geometry: Origin of Quantum Equations" [Dirac 1972, sound recording archived at Xavier University Library, Cincinnati, Ohio; also American Institute of Physics History of Physics catalog icos-28363; and P.A.M. Dirac Collection, Special Collections and Archives, Florida State University Libraries, Tallahassee, Florida]. Verbatim from Dirac's own written notes for the 1972 talk (Florida State University Archives): "There are basically two kinds of math[ematical] thinking, algebraic and geometric. A good mathematician needs to be a master of both. But still he will have a preference for one rather or the other. I prefer the geometric method. Not mentioned in published work because it is not easy to print diagrams. With the algebraic method one deals with equ[ations] between algebraic quantities. Even tho I see the consistency and logical connections of the eq[uations], they do not mean very much to me. I prefer the relationships which I can visualize in geometric terms."*

*Dirac stated at the 1972 Boston talk what the Xavier University Archives catalog record describes as "the personal announcement by Dirac that he had never published his 'secret' use of projective geometry in creating quantum mechanics." Roger Penrose was the moderator of the Boston lecture. After Dirac's presentation of the projective geometry, Penrose asked Dirac to explain how the projective geometry had informed his quantum mechanics. Verbatim from the Woit account of the Farmelo Nature article: "Dirac gave a talk about this at Boston University in 1972, but, after giving a presentation about projective geometry, stopped before explaining the relation to quantum mechanics. Penrose, the moderator, asked Dirac about the relation to quantum mechanics, and in answer 'Dirac gave his trademark shake of the head, and declined to speak.'" The Physics Today profile of Dirac [Farmelo, G., "Paul Dirac, a man apart," Physics Today] gives the same account: "In one telling remark, he said that he had used projective geometry in his earliest papers; he had neglected to mention the mathematics in the papers themselves partly because he thought it was unfamiliar to other physicists... when asked by Roger Penrose at a lecture at Boston University to explain how he had used that geometry in those papers, Dirac refused, gently shaking his head."*

*Scholarly treatments of Dirac's suppressed projective geometry include Peter Galison's "The Suppressed Drawing: Paul Dirac's Hidden Geometry" [Galison, P. 2000, Representations 72, 145-166, Autumn 2000, University of California Press]; Olivier Darrigol's From c-numbers to q-numbers: The Classical Analogy in the History of Quantum Theory [Darrigol, O. 1992, University of California Press, Chapter XI]; and Graham Farmelo's The Strangest Man: The Hidden Life of Paul Dirac [Farmelo, G. 2009, Basic Books]. These sources concur on the historical fact: Dirac's motivations and habitual mode of thinking were geometric (specifically projective-geometric, learned from Peter Fraser at Bristol), while his published presentation was algebraic — and the geometric route was never written down.*

*Scope of this item: what it establishes, what it does not. The Dirac Boston 1972 lecture and its verbatim notes establish primary-source evidence that the physicist who unified matrix mechanics and wave mechanics through transformation theory worked geometrically and published algebraically — with Dirac himself explicitly stating the two-kinds-of-mathematical-thinking dichotomy (algebraic and geometric) and his own preference for the geometric route. This is direct primary-source evidence of the algebra/geometry split at the level of the QM unifier's own methodology, in Dirac's own words, in his own notes for a public lecture. What the 1972 lecture does not establish is what Dirac's specific geometric route was — the reconstruction was not supplied by Dirac (who declined to answer Penrose) and is not supplied by the historical literature. Nothing in the McGucken framework's dual-channel architecture depends on reconstructing Dirac's specific projective-geometric route; the Dirac item is prior-art evidence, in the primary-source words of the QM unifier, that the algebra-versus-geometry dichotomy is not a McGucken imposition on the history but a mode of thinking Dirac explicitly named and preferred while suppressing it in his published work.*

**Remark P.3.3.3 (The general algebra/geometry dichotomy of mathematics per Sir Michael Atiyah, Fields Medal 1966, Abel Prize 2004).** *Sir Michael Atiyah stated the algebra-versus-geometry dichotomy of mathematics as a general fact of the discipline in his article "Special Article: Mathematics in the 20th Century" [Atiyah, M. 2002, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 34, Issue 1, pp. 1-15; based on Atiyah's Fields Institute Toronto lecture of June 2000; also published as Atiyah 2001, American Mathematical Monthly 108(7), 654-666]. Verbatim Atiyah quotations from the 2002 Bulletin article.*

*On the choice as a general fact of mathematical practice: "Should you be an algebraist or a geometer? is like saying Would you rather be deaf or blind?"*

*On the algebraic offer and its cost, in Atiyah's articulation of the geometric-vs-algebraic choice as a live methodological trade: "Algebra is the offer made by the devil to the mathematician. The devil says: 'I will give you this powerful machine, it will answer any question you like. All you need to do is give me your soul: give up geometry and you will have this marvellous machine.'"*

*On the cognitive cost of the algebraic route: "When you pass over into algebraic calculation, essentially you stop thinking; you stop thinking geometrically, you stop thinking about the meaning."*

*Atiyah's 2002 statements are the general-mathematics articulation of the specific-physics dichotomy the McGucken framework identifies as the dual-channel architecture. The algebra/geometry dichotomy is a documented fact about mathematical practice, articulated at Fields-Medal and Abel-Prize level, by a mathematician whose own work spanned both sides (K-theory, index theory, gauge theory). The McGucken framework's contribution is not the identification of the dichotomy — the dichotomy is prior art documented at the general-mathematics level by Atiyah (2002), at the specific-QM level by the Heisenberg-Schrödinger 1925-1926 correspondence and by Dirac's 1972 Boston lecture, and at the historical-mathematics level in the Descartes-1637 unification project. The framework's contribution is the identification that foundational physics inherits this dichotomy as the dual-channel architecture, with dx₄/dt = ic as the source principle from which both channels descend, and with the 47-theorem catalog of §IX.30.C.1 documenting the pattern's ubiquity across QM, GR, thermodynamics, and cosmology.*

**Remark P.3.3.4 (Scope-marking: what the framework's dual-channel claim is not).** *Three items in the surrounding historical and philosophical record are close enough to the framework's dual-channel claim to warrant explicit scope-marking. The framework's claim is different from each of these.*

*(i) The framework's claim is not Bohr complementarity.* Niels Bohr's complementarity principle [Bohr 1928, "The Quantum Postulate and the Recent Development of Atomic Theory," Nature 121, 580-590; also Bohr 1935, "Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?," Physical Review 48, 696-702, the response to Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen] concerns wave/particle and position/momentum as two observational aspects of one system — two ways to interrogate a system with mutually exclusive experimental setups yielding jointly-necessary information. The McGucken framework's dual-channel architecture concerns derivational routes to physical statements — two mathematical apparatuses (algebraic and geometric) that reach the same theorem through disjoint intermediate machinery. The two axes are different. Complementarity is an observational-epistemic distinction about what can be measured jointly (position and momentum cannot be measured together to arbitrary precision; wave and particle behavior appear in mutually exclusive experimental configurations). Dual-channel derivational disjointness is a mathematical-architectural distinction about what mathematical machinery is invoked in the derivation (matrix algebra with Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization is disjoint from Hamilton-Jacobi mechanics with Sturm-Liouville PDE theory). Complementarity operates at the level of the phenomenon; the dual-channel architecture operates at the level of the derivation. The two claims are compatible (both can hold simultaneously in the same physics) but are answering different questions.

*(ii) The framework's claim is not Muller 1997's non-equivalence claim.* Muller 1997 [Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics 28, 35-61 and 219-247, "The equivalence myth of quantum mechanics — Parts I and II"] argues that Schrödinger 1926e's equivalence proof is not foolproof — that the appeal to the moment problem fails, and that at the time of the 1926 proof, matrix mechanics and wave mechanics were neither mathematically nor empirically equivalent. Muller's claim disputes the proof of equivalence. The McGucken framework grants the predictive equivalence of the two formulations (both correctly reproduce the Bohr hydrogen spectrum and the empirical content of QM to the tested precision of contemporary experiment) and asserts derivational disjointness (the two routes to the shared theorems share no intermediate machinery beyond the source principle dx₄/dt = ic and the final theorem). The two claims — Muller's non-equivalence-of-proof claim and the McGucken derivational-disjointness claim — have a common target: the historical tradition's premature closure of the question after the 1926 equivalence proofs, which precluded further investigation into whether the two routes descend from a common source principle upstream of both. Muller's claim disputes the closure at the level of the proof; the McGucken framework accepts the predictive equivalence at the empirical level and disputes the closure at the level of the derivational content, asking the question the 1926-1932 tradition did not ask: does a physical statement upstream of both routes generate both as consequences via disjoint intermediate machinery?

*(iii) The framework's claim is not one-notation-for-one-theory.* The 1926 equivalence proofs by Schrödinger, Eckart, Pauli, and later formalized by Dirac 1927 (transformation theory) and von Neumann 1932 (abstract Hilbert-space formulation) are often summarized as "there is one quantum mechanics in two notations" — matrix notation and wave-function notation as interchangeable presentations of the same underlying theory. This summary is the closure the framework disputes. Equivalence of formalism is the opposite claim from derivational disjointness. Equivalence-of-formalism says the machinery is interchangeable, the two notations translate cleanly into each other. Derivational disjointness says the two routes to the shared theorems share no intermediate machinery, and only the source principle and the final theorem are shared. The 1926-1932 closure was that the machinery is interchangeable and therefore the question ends. The framework's claim is that the derivational routes are disjoint and therefore the question opens — what physical statement upstream of both generates them both as consequences via disjoint routes? The framework's answer is dx₄/dt = ic.

*(iv) The framework does not claim convergent overdetermination itself as novel.* The 1925-1926 Heisenberg-Schrödinger case is prior art for the convergent-overdetermination pattern, not just for the algebra/geometry framing. The Bohr hydrogen spectrum was reached twice from different empirical starting-data through different mathematical apparatuses by investigators with different training within twelve months, with nobody intending the double derivation. Wimsatt-style convergent overdetermination as an evidential mode is therefore documented at one QM theorem in 1925-1926 (formalized only after the fact by Schrödinger 1926e's equivalence paper and von Neumann 1932's Hilbert-space rigorization) and does not require the McGucken framework to introduce it. What the framework claims is narrower and checkable at the technical level: (a) the convergence is systematic across 47 theorems rather than accidental at one; (b) both routes descend from a single identified source principle dx₄/dt = ic; (c) the derivational disjointness at each theorem is verifiable via the Dual-Channel Disjointness Predicate of Definition IX.26.2 of §IX.26 above. The phenomenon of two-derivations-converging-on-one-theorem at the founding of QM is prior art; the systematic recurrence across 47 theorems and the identification of the upstream source principle are the framework's contributions. Full scope-marking of what the framework does and does not claim as novel appears in the Scope-marking paragraph of Remark IX.30.C.1.3 in the 47-theorem catalog section below.

*(v) What the historical record contains, and what it does not.* Across the primary sources (Schrödinger 1926a-d, Schrödinger 1926e, Heisenberg 1925, Born-Jordan 1925, Born-Heisenberg-Jordan 1926, Dirac 1927 transformation theory, Heisenberg 1927 uncertainty, Bohr 1928 complementarity, Dirac 1930 Principles of Quantum Mechanics, von Neumann 1932 Mathematische Grundlagen, Dirac 1965 "Quantum Electrodynamics without Dead Wood," Dirac 1972 Boston lecture) and the historical-philosophical secondary literature (Muller 1997, Madrid-Casado 2008, Perović 2008, Johnson-Freyd 2021, Bédard 2025, Connes 2000, Galison 2000, Darrigol 1992, Farmelo 2009, Atiyah 2002 on the general-mathematics dichotomy, SEP articles on the Uncertainty Principle and Copenhagen Interpretation, Weinstein 2025 arXiv 2511.07502), the two derivational routes to the QM canon are named, contrasted, valued, proved formally equivalent (Schrödinger 1926e, Eckart 1926, Dirac 1927, von Neumann 1932), disputed as to foolproofness (Muller 1997, Perović 2008), extended to a categorical inequivalence in the QFT case (Johnson-Freyd 2021, Haag 1955, and Dirac himself in 1965: "the Heisenberg picture is a good picture, the Schrödinger picture is a bad picture, and the two pictures are not equivalent"), extended to a realism-based inequivalence at the ontological level (Bédard 2025: "descriptors surject onto but do not reduce to the Schrödinger state"), argued over as to the status of visualizability (Schrödinger-Heisenberg correspondence 1926, Bohr-Heisenberg dispute at 1927 Solvay Conference), and explicitly named by Dirac in 1972 as two kinds of mathematical thinking with his own geometric preference kept out of the published work. What is not present in the historical record: a physical statement upstream of both routes from which both derive as consequences, together with a proof of derivational disjointness of the two routes descending from that common upstream principle. The record supplies the phenomenon (two derivations, convergent on empirical predictions in the finite-dimensional case, divergent at the QFT and ontological levels, from different starting points and different mathematical apparatuses) without supplying the explanation (the upstream source principle from which both descend). The McGucken framework's identification of dx₄/dt = ic as the upstream principle and the 47-theorem dual catalog of §IX.30.C.1 as the derivational-disjointness proof is what the record does not supply — and this is the specific contribution of the framework beyond the 1926-1932 formalization and the century of scholarly discussion that followed.*

**Remark P.3.3.5 (The channel-forcing argument: each investigator's empirical starting-data and mathematical training forced the channel).** *Neither Heisenberg nor Schrödinger chose a channel. Each took the problem that his position at Munich or Zurich had handed him, with the mathematical training that his fifteen years' or five years' prior apprenticeship had given him, and arrived at one derivational route without the other in view. The channel each ended up developing was forced by the empirical starting-data and the mathematical training in combination. This is the substantive content behind the historical asymmetries documented in Remark P.3.3.1 above; the present remark states the forcing mechanism explicitly.*

*(i) The two-index-amplitude data forced matrix algebra.* Heisenberg's July 1925 paper worked with quantities indexed by pairs of atomic stationary states — the amplitude for the transition $n \to m$ is a two-index object $a_{nm}$, and the Ritz combination principle of Ritz 1908 (which regulates which pairs of spectral-line frequencies add to give another spectral-line frequency) requires that composing two such transition amplitudes in succession sums over intermediate states: $(AB)_{ik} = \sum_j A_{ij} B_{jk}$. Heisenberg wrote down this composition rule from the observational data and found that the resulting product does not commute in general. He did not recognize the mathematical structure. Recognition came only after Heisenberg mailed the manuscript from Helgoland to Göttingen: Born recognized it, per Madrid-Casado 2008 verbatim, when he "suddenly remembered an algebraic theory which he had learned from his [former teacher, Jakob Rosanes]." Jordan supplied the systematic formalization in Born-Jordan 1925. The forcing chain is: (a) atomic spectroscopy delivers frequencies and intensities indexed by pairs of stationary states; (b) the Ritz combination principle regulates which pairs compose; (c) a quantity indexed by a pair with the Ritz composition rule is a two-index object with sum-over-intermediates multiplication; (d) that structure is the algebra of matrices. The data forced the algebraic channel. Connes 2000 [arXiv math/0011193] states the forcing chain verbatim: "quantum mechanics showed that indeed the parameter space, or phase space of the mechanical system given by a single atom fails to be a manifold... dictated by the *experimental findings of spectroscopy*."

*(ii) The standing-wave-boundary data forced PDEs on a continuum.* Schrödinger's four papers of 1926 worked with a quantity that is a wave field defined on a continuous configuration space, quantized by requiring that the field satisfy boundary conditions at spatial infinity (bound states) or asymptotic conditions (scattering states). The Bohr atomic energy levels appear as eigenvalues of the operator $-(\hbar^2/2m)\nabla^2 + V(x)$ acting on square-integrable functions $\psi(x)$ satisfying appropriate boundary conditions. The paper series is titled *Quantisierung als Eigenwertproblem* — "Quantization as an Eigenvalue Problem." Schrödinger had spent his fifteen years of pre-QM work in exactly this kind of problem: Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue theory of PDEs, wave propagation and interference in continuous media, vibrational theory of continuous mechanical systems, statistical continuum thermodynamics. The forcing chain is: (a) the de Broglie matter-wave hypothesis (transmitted to Schrödinger via Einstein 1924-25, see (iii) below) delivers a wave field associated with a material particle; (b) quantization of the wave field by boundary conditions is an eigenvalue problem for a differential operator; (c) an eigenvalue problem for a differential operator on a continuous configuration space is Sturm-Liouville PDE theory. The data forced the geometric-wave channel. Where Heisenberg needed Born to supply the algebra he had unwittingly reinvented, Schrödinger needed Weyl to help complete the analysis of an equation whose frame was native to him from fifteen years of prior work. Verbatim from a Schrödinger letter of late 1925 (per Renn 2013, "Schrödinger and the Genesis of Wave Mechanics"): "At the moment I am struggling with a new atomic theory. If only I knew more mathematics! I am very optimistic about this thing, and expect that, if only I can... solve it, it will be very beautiful... At present I must learn a little mathematics in order to completely solve the vibration problem." Schrödinger's colleague Hermann Weyl at ETH Zurich — Schrödinger's senior by only two years, in "regular communication" per the historical record [arXiv math/0409571, "Introducing Groups into Quantum Theory (1926-1930)"] — supplied the mathematical assistance. Verbatim from arXiv 1203.3678 ("Do We Understand Quantum Mechanics — Finally?"): "It was Weyl who apparently explained to Schrödinger that his time-independent wave equation represented an eigenvalue problem and directed him to the right mathematical literature. Schrödinger acknowledges this in his first paper on wave mechanics."

*(iii) The Einstein 1924-25 transmission channel from de Broglie to Schrödinger.* The de Broglie matter-wave hypothesis reached Schrödinger not directly from de Broglie's 1924 Paris thesis but through Einstein's two papers on the quantum theory of the ideal gas — Einstein 1924 ["Quantentheorie des einatomigen idealen Gases," Preuss. Ak. Wiss. Sitzb. 1924, pp. 261-267] and Einstein 1925 ["Quantentheorie des einatomigen idealen Gases, Zweite Abhandlung," Preuss. Ak. Wiss. Sitzb. 1925, pp. 3-14]. Einstein had received de Broglie's Paris thesis from Langevin, and Einstein 1925 cited de Broglie's thesis. Einstein's verbatim endorsement, from Einstein 1925 (Doc. 385 of the Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Volume 14): "I believe that this is more than a mere analogy; de Broglie has shown in a very important work how a (scalar) wave field can be coordinated with a material particle or a system of material particles." Einstein to Lorentz, 16 December 1924 (Doc. 399 of Collected Papers Vol. 14): "A younger brother of the de Broglie known to us has made a very interesting attempt to interpret the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rules (Paris Dissertation, 1924). I believe that it is the first feeble ray of light to illuminate this, the worst of our physical riddles. I have also discovered something that supports his construction." Schrödinger read Einstein 1925 in mid-1925, was suspicious of the "unnatural" way of counting states used by Einstein and Bose, and — per the historical record — sought a more "natural" wave-based route to the same statistical content. The Einstein-Schrödinger correspondence of late 1925 (documented in Howard 1990 and Renn 2013) is the transmission channel by which de Broglie's matter waves reached Schrödinger; the immediate proximate cause of Schrödinger's writing down the wave equation was Debye's Zurich-seminar prompt of November 1925, but the underlying theoretical commitment was to Einstein-endorsed de Broglie waves. As of January 1926, when Schrödinger submitted his first wave-mechanics paper to Annalen der Physik (27 January 1926 per Schrödinger 1926a), de Broglie's matter waves had no direct experimental confirmation — the Davisson-Germer experiment demonstrating electron diffraction from a nickel crystal came in 1927 [Davisson, C.J., and Germer, L.H. 1927, "Diffraction of Electrons by a Crystal of Nickel," Physical Review 30, 705-740], after Schrödinger's wave equation was published and after Heisenberg's uncertainty paper of the same year. Schrödinger started from a theoretical hypothesis (transmitted through Einstein's endorsement) rather than from direct measurement; Heisenberg started from spectroscopic measurement (transition amplitudes read from atomic-emission photographic plates).

*(iv) The biographical asymmetry that positioned each investigator at a different downstream projection.* In July 1925, when Heisenberg wrote the *Umdeutung* paper on Helgoland, he was 23 years old, with a Munich doctorate of 1923 titled *Über Stabilität und Turbulenz von Flüssigkeitsströmen* ("On the Stability and Turbulence of Fluid Flow") under Arnold Sommerfeld [Heisenberg 1923, 59-page dissertation, submitted 10 June 1923, defended 23 July 1923, University of Munich; per AIP History of Physics Web Exhibit "The Sad Story of Heisenberg's Doctorate" and Lynge offprint records]. Sommerfeld's evaluation of the thesis: "I would not have proposed a topic of this difficulty as a dissertation to any of my other pupils." Heisenberg's subsequent training was in atomic spectroscopy at Göttingen with Born (habilitation 1924) and Copenhagen with Bohr (1924-1925 Rockefeller fellowship). His scientific formation was: (a) five years of formal training (1920-1925) concentrated in atomic-spectroscopic apprenticeship in the Bohr-Sommerfeld tradition; (b) prior collaboration with Kramers on the Kramers-Heisenberg dispersion formula of 1924-1925, which set the classical action-angle-variable framework he later re-interpreted; (c) a doctoral dissertation in hydrodynamics that Sommerfeld had specifically assigned as a traditional-topic counterweight to Heisenberg's reputation for "controversial solutions to problems in quantum theory" (per AIP History of Physics). In January 1926, when Schrödinger completed his first wave-mechanics paper, he was 38 years old, with a Vienna doctorate of 1910 under Franz-Serafin Exner and Friedrich Hasenöhrl, followed by fifteen years of published work in classical continuum and statistical physics: vibrational theory of continuous mechanical systems, Brownian motion, dielectrics, colour perception, statistical mechanics of gases, and general relativity. His scientific formation was: (a) five years of doctoral training in the Vienna continuum-physics tradition (1906-1910); (b) fifteen years of subsequent research in continuous-medium problems where PDE eigenvalue theory and boundary-value analysis were the daily working mathematics; (c) the Zurich Chair of Theoretical Physics (from 1921) placing him at the center of Debye's joint University-ETH seminar and in mathematical collaboration-distance from Hermann Weyl at ETH.

*The biographical asymmetry places each investigator at a different downstream projection of the underlying physics. Heisenberg — 23, Munich-Göttingen-Copenhagen spectroscopic apprentice, prior collaboration on Kramers dispersion, five years of formal training — hit the two-index-amplitude-with-Ritz-composition data first and reached for the mathematics that data forced (matrix algebra, once Born supplied recognition). Schrödinger — 38, Vienna continuum-physics veteran, fifteen years of PDE eigenvalue and vibrational-theory work, Weyl-collaboration-distance — hit the de Broglie-Einstein wave-field hypothesis first (transmitted via Einstein 1925 and Debye's seminar prompt) and reached for the mathematics that hypothesis forced (Sturm-Liouville PDE eigenvalue theory on continuous configuration space, once Weyl supplied the analytic assistance). Neither man chose a channel: each took the problem his position handed him with the mathematics his training had given him, and arrived at one derivational route without the other in view.*

*(v) Epistemic scope-marking of what the historical case establishes and what it does not.* The framework's derivational-disjointness claim of §IX.30.C.1 does not require this reading of the Heisenberg-Schrödinger history, and this reading of the Heisenberg-Schrödinger history does not establish the framework's claim. The framework's claim is a mathematical-architectural fact about the 47 theorems of the dual catalog, supported at the technical level by the derivational-disjointness predicate of Definition IX.26.2 and verified theorem-by-theorem in [3, §II-III]. The historical case is separate evidence of a different character. What the historical case does supply: (a) documented primary-source evidence that at the birth of QM in 1925-1926, two derivations descended from disjoint mathematical apparatuses starting from different empirical starting-data and reaching the same shared physics; (b) documented primary-source evidence (Dirac 1972 Boston lecture per Remark P.3.3.2 above) that the physicist who unified the two formulations through transformation theory worked geometrically while publishing algebraically; (c) documented primary-source evidence (Atiyah 2002 per Remark P.3.3.3 above) that the algebra-versus-geometry dichotomy is a general fact of mathematical practice articulated at the Fields-Medal level. What the historical case does not supply: a derivation of the framework's specific theorems, an independent proof of the derivational-disjointness predicate, or a demonstration that dx₄/dt = ic is the source principle. The relationship between the historical case and the framework's claim is asymmetric and one-directional: if the framework's claim is correct (two derivational channels descending from one source via disjoint intermediate machinery), then the historical asymmetries documented in Remarks P.3.3.1 through P.3.3.5 above are exactly what one should expect to find at the founding of QM — two investigators positioned at different downstream projections of the underlying physics, each reconstructing with the tools that projection demands, arriving at formally equivalent but derivationally disjoint routes. The historical asymmetries (Munich atomic spectroscopy against Vienna continuum physics; 23 against 38; five years of formal training against twenty years; transition-amplitude intensity data against de Broglie matter-wave hypothesis transmitted via Einstein; Born's post-hoc algebraic recognition against Weyl's contemporaneous analytic collaboration) are the historical trace of the derivational disjointness that §IX.30.C.1's 47-theorem catalog documents theorem-by-theorem at the technical level. The historical case is confirmatory rather than derivational: it is what the framework's picture predicts about the historical record, not what the framework's picture is built from.*

### P.3.4 Hertz 1894's documented stripping of Maxwell's geometry

Maxwell 1865/1873 supplied the geometric-mechanical-ether reading of electromagnetism with twenty equations in scalar and quaternion components. Heaviside 1880s and Hertz 1890s stripped Maxwell's geometry and reformulated as four duplex algebraic vector-calculus equations. By 1894, Hertz had completed the algebraic stripping. Hertz documented this in his own primary-source writings (*Electric Waves*, 1893). This is the canonical pre-quantum case of the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel-suppression-of-dx₄/dt=ic the Geometric Channel, documented in real time by the figure who did the stripping. The textbook electromagnetism every physics undergraduate learns is Hertz's the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel formulation; Maxwell's original the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel formulation is treated as historical curiosity.

### P.3.5 Bohr 1927's complementarity

Bohr's complementarity principle is the closest pre-McGucken articulation of the dual-channel architecture as a philosophical-claim. Wave and particle descriptions are complementary; you cannot use both simultaneously; both are needed for a complete description; the measurement apparatus determines which applies. Bohr treated complementarity as a fundamental rather than as evidence of a deeper geometric source. He had the duck-rabbit framing that Tong 2024 recovers; he did not have the source principle.

### P.3.6 Einstein 1905-1935's QM/GR channel split

Einstein chose the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel for the photoelectric effect ($E = h\nu$, discrete quanta, algebraic-energy reading) in 1905 and the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel for general relativity (geometric metric, curvature, geodesics) in 1915. The channel split lived in Einstein's own work for 30 years. His EPR 1935 objection to QM was a dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel-geometric concern about realism that he had supplied for GR but not for QM. The poignant : Einstein wrote $x_4 = ict$ in his notation from 1908 onward (following Minkowski) and never recognized that the $ict$ was the integrated form of an active expansion at velocity c — dx₄/dt = ic was sitting in his notation, and he did not see it.

Hilbert derived the Einstein field equations from a variational principle (the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel) in 1915. Eighty years later, Jacobson derived the same equations from horizon thermodynamics on local Rindler horizons (the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel) in 1995, with no shared intermediate machinery. Bekenstein-Hawking entropy $S_{BH} = k_B A/(4\ell_P^2)$ plus Unruh temperature $T_U = \hbar a/(2\pi c k_B)$ plus Clausius relation $\delta Q = T\,dS$ plus Raychaudhuri focusing producing $G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = (8\pi G/c^4) T_{\mu\nu}$ as an equation of state. The two derivations are independent and converge on the same equations because both read the same physics of dx₄/dt = ic at the gravitational tier through two disjoint chains. Neither Hilbert nor Jacobson identified the agreement as evidence of an underlying foundational principle; Jacobson treated his derivation as a thermodynamic curiosity ("an equation of state"). The McGucken framework recognizes the Hilbert-Jacobson agreement as single demonstration of the dual-channel architecture (Corollary IX.15.6), with eleven subsequent emergent-gravity programmes (Verlinde 2011, Padmanabhan 2010s, FGHMVR 2014, Cao-Carroll 2017, and the others enumerated in Table IX.25.B.A) classified as the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel subsets each instantiating the same horizon-thermodynamics.

## P.4 What Makes the McGucken Duality Unprecedented

Across 250 years of foundational physics — from Newton's *Principia* (1687) through Maxwell's *Treatise* (1873), Einstein's papers (1905-1955), Bohr's complementarity (1927), Hamilton-Lagrange (1834-1843), Heisenberg-Schrödinger (1925-1926), Feynman-Dyson (1948-1949), Wheeler-Feynman (1945), Jacobson (1995), the eight emergent-spacetime programmes (1967-2026), and the contemporary Harlow-Turok-Tong articulations (2024-2026) — many figures came close to the McGucken Duality without crossing the threshold. Each prior figure had one or two pieces of the dual-channel architecture. None had all five pieces together:

**(P.4.1) The single physical principle from which both channels descend.** Hamilton-Lagrange had the duality empirically; they had no source principle. Heisenberg-Schrödinger had the equivalence; they had no source principle. Feynman-Dyson had the path-integral / canonical equivalence; they had no source principle. Hilbert-Jacobson had the GR-tier convergence; they had no source principle. Einstein, Wheeler, Penrose, Maldacena, Verlinde, Van Raamsdonk, Arkani-Hamed-Trnka, Witten — none identified what physics is descending from. The McGucken framework supplies dx₄/dt = ic as the source.

**(P.4.2) The physics of the principle as a wavefront-advance with wavelength, frequency, phase, and action.** Even with the principle on the table, the physics, that x₄ expands as a spherically symmetric wavefront at velocity c carrying wavelength, frequency, phase, and therefore action (§I.1 Items I.1.S.1-I.1.S.4) — supplies the wavefront-based foundation from which $c$ and $\hbar$ become twin properties of one advance, the spinor lives on a wavefront that already has the Compton frequency, and the dynamics are in the premise. No prior framework articulated the McGucken Principle's physics as a wavefront-advance.

**(P.4.3) The 2×N matrix of dual-channel theorems.** No prior framework articulated more than one or two disjoint dual derivations. The McGucken corpus articulates 47 theorems with 94 derivations total, spanning the full breadth of foundational physics.

**(P.4.4) The derivational-disjointness predicate and Bayesian likelihood ratio.** No prior framework articulated the formal diagnostic by which two derivations are recognized as disjoint, nor the Bayesian-evidentiary argument that 47 disjoint-derivation agreements supply $\geq 10^{141}$ likelihood ratio in favor of the source.

**(P.4.5) The coordinate-identification bridge and differential response.** No prior framework identified the McGucken-Wick rotation $\tau = x_4/c$ as a coordinate identification on the real four-manifold $\mathcal M_G$; the standard treatment is as a formal analytic continuation on a complex $t$-plane. No prior framework articulated the differential response of the two channels to the rotation as the diagnostic of their derivational disjointness.

## P.5 The Deep

The McGucken Duality is the pattern that 250 years of foundational physics has been articulating in fragments, with the McGucken framework supplying the source principle that makes the fragments coherent. Hamilton-Lagrange had the classical-mechanical fragment; Heisenberg-Schrödinger had the quantum-mechanical fragment; Maxwell-Hertz had the electromagnetic fragment with documented suppression-history; Hilbert-Jacobson had the gravitational fragment; Einstein had the channel split in his own work without resolving it; Bohr had the complementarity philosophical fragment; Feynman-Dyson had the QFT fragment; Wheeler had the methodology and the "it from bit" intuition without dx₄/dt = ic; the eight emergent-spacetime programmes had the empirical convergence on "spacetime is emergent" without identifying what it emerges from; Harlow-Turok-Tong articulate the contemporary unresolved-foundational-questions fragment.

Each fragment, in isolation, looked like a curious feature of the local subfield. The McGucken Duality recognizes that the fragments are all readings of one fact — the physics of dx₄/dt = ic as a wavefront-advance generating two distinct sets of properties simultaneously, and assembles the fragments into the coherent dual-channel architecture.

The historical pattern is uniform and contemporaneous. Five primary-source documentations exhibit the pattern: Schrödinger 1926b for Hamilton, Hertz 1894 for Maxwell, Harlow 2026 for contemporary quantum gravity, Turok 2024 for contemporary cosmology, Tong 2024 for contemporary quantum field theory — record the figures who lived through the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel-suppressing-dx₄/dt=ic the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel pattern in real time. The suppression of the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel in favor of the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel has been documented contemporaneously across five distinct historical moments by five different figures across three centuries. The dual-channel architecture is a observed by the figures themselves. The McGucken framework's contribution is the recognition that every prior dual-content sighting is a special case of the dual-channel architecture forced by the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic.

The McGucken Duality is, in the sense, what foundational physics IS — the fingerprint of dx₄/dt = ic at every level of theory.

- **Physically**, the McGucken Duality is that x₄'s active expansion at velocity c as a spherically symmetric wavefront from every event has both algebraic-spectral content (the phase advance carrying action quantum ℏ per cycle, articulating the dx₄/dt=ic Algebraic Channel's operator-algebraic / symmetry-group content) and geometric-propagation (the spatial Sphere shape evolving under spherical-symmetric expansion at c, articulating the dx₄/dt=ic Geometric Channel's Huygens / Bekenstein-Hawking / FLRW content) simultaneously, with both contents being components of one physical reality.

- **Mathematically**, the McGucken Duality is that every theorem of foundational physics admits two disjoint derivations from dx₄/dt = ic, with the 47-theorem dual-channel architecture supplying 94 derivations and the Bayesian likelihood ratio $\geq 10^{141}$ supplying evidentiary force for the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic.

- **Historically**, the McGucken Duality is the pattern that 250 years of foundational physics has been articulating in fragments — from Hamilton-Lagrange through Maxwell-Hertz, Heisenberg-Schrödinger, Einstein's channel split, Bohr's complementarity, Hilbert-Jacobson, Feynman-Dyson, Wheeler's "it from bit", the eight emergent-spacetime programmes, and Harlow-Turok-Tong's contemporary triple-articulation, with the McGucken framework supplying the source principle dx₄/dt = ic that makes the fragments coherent into a single dual-channel architecture.
